newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan seen over-confident on IMF support.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan seen over-confident on IMF support.

text.p: Pakistan's interim government is keen to save an ailing economy and launch structural reforms, but its public assertions that generous IMF support will help rebuild reserves fast could backfire, bankers said on Tuesday.

President Farooq Leghari said on Monday that liquid foreign reserves, which touched a year-low of $570 million on October 31 before climbing back to $630 million a week later, were expected to reach $1 billion by the end of December.

"I hope this will restore the confidence of savers and investors," he told a news conference. He said Pakistan had been in danger of defaulting on its foreign debt before he sacked Benazir Bhutto's government on November 5.

Bankers say bringing reserves back to $1 billion will be no easy task given debt payments of more than $500 million due in December and a substantial trade deficit. The trade gap widened to $443 million in October from $415 million in September.
"The $1 billion target is difficult as inflows are slow while the trade deficit is alarming," said Masooq Ahmed, vice president of the private Muslim Commercial bank.
Shahid Javed Burki, finance and economic affairs adviser to the prime minister, has said he plans to go to Washington early next month for talks with the International Monetary Fund.

A visiting IMF mission last week agreed to recommend the reactivation of a stalled $600 million standby loan, with two tranches of $80 million each to be released once the IMF's board approves the latest agreement with Pakistan by mid-December.
The IMF also agreed to consider a Pakistani request for more money to be made available under the standby arrangement.
Burki said he expected the IMF to make an upfront payment on top of the $160 million in delayed tranches and Leghari also announced that additional money would be forthcoming.
However, the IMF has made no commitment to expand the loan.

Burki has set up task forces to propose reforms in banking, fiscal policy, tariff reform, taxation, industry, agriculture and other areas. Their reports, due by the end of this month, are to form the basis of a new structural reform programme.
Leghari said the IMF had agreed to start talks on an enhanced structural adjustment facility (ESAF).
"A new ESAF may be possible within the period of the interim government," he said.
The caretaker government has only three months in power before supervising general elections set for February 3.
The IMF had earlier envisaged starting ESAF talks in February or March, with the actual lending programme beginning in 1997/98, the fiscal year that starts on July 1.

Economists said it was unlikely that there would be time to reach an ESAF agreement before the elections. The IMF would be reluctant to start any new lending until Pakistan had shown it could meet its commitments under the standby deal.
"The government wants its reforms publicly announced to try to prevent any new government from backtracking," an independent economist said. "But how far can the IMF go along with that?"
The IMF is known to be concerned about the degree to which any incoming elected government will feel itself bound by agreements reached by the caretaker administration.

Leghari has promised to ensure continuity, but both main parties, Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party and the Pakistan Muslim League led by Nawaz Sharif, have said they would scrutinise any deal with the IMF if voted into power.

To boost reserves, the State (central) Bank of Pakistan has wooed foreign deposits by offering high rates of return on funds placed in a special central bank account. This week it extended the deadline for such deposits to December 10 from November 28.
Umar Ehtesham, forex analyst at Banque Indosuez, said several foreign banks were scrambling to arrange forex deposits from abroad to benefit from the central bank's offer.

Economists said the central bank was caught in a dilemma between the need to rebuild foreign reserves to a comfortable level and the longer-term objective of reducing the proportion of costly short-term borrowing in the overall debt structure.

"The danger is that having set a target of $1 billion, even if they get reserves up to $800 or $900 million, the market will see it as falling short -- and they could start window-dressing with short-term loans or delaying import payments," one said.
